title: An Introduction to mise, the Multi-Language Version Manager
summary: See how mise manages Node and Python versions per project, handles existing version files, locks tools, sets environment variables, and runs consistent builds locally and in CI.
body_markdown:
mise is a single command-line tool that installs and switches versions of Node, Python, Ruby and other runtimes per directory, reading them from a` mise.toml` file at the project root.


If your repo has a Vite frontend and a Python script that generates content before the build, you are probably running nvm and pyenv side by side and hoping every teammate’s shell agrees with CI. Usually one of them doesn’t.


For a side-by-side look at mise, nvm, pyenv, rustup and SDKMAN!, see[5 Version Managers Every Developer Should Know](https://blog.openreplay.com/5-version-managers-developers/) . This article skips the feature list. Instead it takes one repo and follows it through` cd` , existing` .nvmrc` files, a teammate’s first clone, CI, a two-runtime build task and env vars.


## Key Takeaways


- With shell activation, entering a directory that has a` mise.toml` puts that project’s pinned runtimes on PATH, and leaving it restores the previous versions.
- mise ignores` .nvmrc` and` .python-version` unless you turn them on per tool with the` idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools` setting.
- ` mise run` loads the project’s tools and env itself and installs missing tools by default, so it works in CI without shell activation.
- ` jdx/mise-action@v4` installs mise and the tools in` mise.toml` . If a` mise.lock` is committed, it installs with` --locked` .
- The` \[env\]` table is plain text that gets committed. It is for configuration, not secrets.


## The Project: A Vite Frontend With a Python Build Step


The example repo,` docs-preview` , has two runtimes, one config file and one workflow:


```text
docs-preview/
├── content/*.md
├── scripts/build_content.py
├── src/
├── package.json          # vite in devDependencies
├── mise.toml
└── .github/workflows/build.yml
```


The Python script uses only the standard library. It turns the Markdown files into JSON that the frontend imports:


```text
# scripts/build_content.py
import   json, os, pathlib


src   =   pathlib.Path(os.environ.get(  "  CONTENT_DIR  "  ,   "  content  "  ))
out   =   pathlib.Path(  "  src/generated/content.json  "  )
out.parent.mkdir(  parents  =  True  ,   exist_ok  =  True  )


items   =   [{  "  slug  "  : p.stem,   "  body  "  : p.read_text(  encoding  =  "  utf-8  "  )}
for   p   in   sorted  (src.glob(  "  *.md  "  ))]
out.write_text(json.dumps(items,   indent  =  2  ),   encoding  =  "  utf-8  "  )
print  (  f  "wrote   {  len  (items)  }   items to   {  out  }  "  )
```


This is the full` mise.toml` . Later sections refer back to it:


```text
[  tools  ]
node   =   "  24  "
python   =   "  3.14  "


[  settings  ]
lockfile   =   true


[  env  ]
CONTENT_DIR   =   "  content  "
VITE_SITE_NAME   =   "  Docs Preview  "


[  tasks  .  install  ]
description   =   "  Install JS dependencies  "
run   =   "  npm ci  "


[  tasks  .  "build:content"  ]
description   =   "  Convert content files to JSON for the frontend  "
run   =   "  python scripts/build_content.py  "


[  tasks  .  build  ]
description   =   "  Generate content, then build the Vite app  "
depends   = [  "  install  "  ,   "  build:content  "  ]
run   =   "  npx vite build  "
```


The` \[tools\]` table uses version prefixes (Node 24 LTS, Python 3.14). The lockfile, covered below, records the exact patch versions they resolve to.


## What Happens When You cd In and Out


With mise activated, entering a directory that contains a` mise.toml` puts that project’s pinned runtimes on your PATH. Leaving it restores whatever versions were active before. Once[mise activate](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/activate.html) is in your shell startup file, mise swaps tools and environment variables each time you change directory.


```text
cd   ~
node   --version          # whatever your system or nvm provides
cd   ~/code/docs-preview
node   --version          # v24.x from mise.toml
python3   --version       # Python 3.14.x
echo   "  $CONTENT_DIR  "     # content
```


When mise switches versions depends on the shell. Per the[shims documentation](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/shims.html) , bash, zsh, fish and xonsh switch as soon as you run` cd` . Other shells wait until the next prompt appears.


### When a Pinned Version Isn’t Installed Yet


On a fresh machine, run` mise install` in the project directory. That is the explicit, predictable fix. Tasks also handle it for you:[mise tasks](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/) run with the project’s tools and env vars, and the` auto_install` setting, which is on by default, installs any missing configured tools when you call` mise run` . Python needs care if you rely on shims. The[settings reference](https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration/settings.html) explains that a shim which can’t resolve a mise-managed version (for example, when auto-install is turned off) falls back to the first program with the same name elsewhere on PATH. For a tool the OS also ships, like` python3` , that means your pinned version never runs and you get no error.


To pin a different version in one terminal only, use[mise shell node@<version>](https://mise.jdx.dev/cli/shell.html) . This needs a shell where mise is already activated.


## Existing .nvmrc and .python-version Files


mise does not read` .nvmrc` or` .python-version` unless you turn it on for each tool with` idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools` . The[mise FAQ](https://mise.jdx.dev/faq.html) confirms these idiomatic version files are off by default. That default arrived in[mise 2025.10.0](https://github.com/jdx/mise/releases/tag/v2025.10.0) . To opt in:


```text
[  settings  ]
idiomatic_version_file_enable_tools   = [  "  node  "  ,   "  python  "  ]
```


The[configuration docs](https://mise.jdx.dev/configuration.html) list` package.json` among the files mise reads for` node` , so enabling` node` can pick that file up too. To skip a single file, add a` tool:filename` pair such as` node:package.json` to the` idiomatic_version_file_disable_files` setting.


Once` mise.toml` pins both runtimes, keep` .nvmrc` only for teammates still on nvm, and make sure the two files agree. If you need a refresher on how nvm treats that file, see the guides for switching Node versions with nvm on[macOS](https://blog.openreplay.com/switch-nodejs-versions-macos-nvm/) ,[Linux](https://blog.openreplay.com/switch-nodejs-versions-linux-nvm/) and[Windows](https://blog.openreplay.com/switch-nodejs-versions-windows-nvm/) .


## Teammates and CI


A laptop and a CI runner read the same` mise.toml` but get tools onto PATH in different ways:


Laptop GitHub Actions


Tools on PATH Activation hook in the shell` jdx/mise-action` installs mise and pinned tools


Version source` mise.toml` +` mise.lock` Same files


Build command` mise run build`` mise run build`


**A teammate’s first clone:**


1. Install mise:` curl https://mise.run | sh`
2. Add` eval "$(~/.local/bin/mise activate zsh)"` (or the line for your shell) to your shell rc file.
3. Review` mise.toml` , then run` mise install` .
4. Run` mise run build` .


mise’s trust model needs care because config files can execute code. According to the[getting-started guide](https://mise.jdx.dev/getting-started.html) , outside CI and paranoid mode, any command that acts on the project, such as` mise install` ,` mise exec` or` mise run` , trusts the active config automatically. So review` mise.toml` before you run one, and use` mise trust` when you want to trust a config explicitly.


**Lock exact versions.** The[lockfile](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/mise-lock.html) ,` mise.lock` , is created by` mise lock` or by the` lockfile = true` setting shown above. Commit it. With` mise install --locked` , a missing lock entry becomes an error, so mise never quietly picks a new version.


**CI workflow:**


```text
# .github/workflows/build.yml
name  :   build
on  : [  push  ,   pull_request  ]
jobs  :
build  :
runs-on  :   ubuntu-latest
steps  :
-   uses  :   actions/checkout@v6
-   uses  :   jdx/mise-action@v4
-   run  :   mise run build
```


The[mise-action](https://github.com/jdx/mise-action) step installs mise and the tools in` mise.toml` , so the workflow uses the same versions developers use locally. By default it runs` mise install` (` install: true` ) and caches tools (` cache: true` ). When` mise.lock` is present, it installs with` --locked` . It also passes` ${{ github.token }}` automatically. On laptops, setting` GITHUB_TOKEN` or` MISE_GITHUB_TOKEN` helps if installs hit rate limits, as described on the[GitHub tokens page](https://mise.jdx.dev/dev-tools/github-tokens.html) .


**When something breaks** , three commands narrow it down:


Symptom Command


Activation or install looks wrong` mise doctor`


Wrong config file seems to apply` mise config ls`


Wrong version selected` mise ls --current`


## A Real Task: mise run build Across Two Runtimes


A task defined in` mise.toml` runs with the project’s pinned tools and` \[env\]` variables already applied. That means` mise run build` uses the same Node and Python on a laptop and in CI, even without shell activation.


The` depends` key makes` build` wait until every task it lists has finished, so the Python step has written` src/generated/content.json` before Vite reads it. The listed tasks can run concurrently. The tasks docs state that prerequisites may run in parallel, and that their order in` depends` does not establish a sequence. That is safe here because` npm ci` writes` node_modules` and the Python script writes` src/generated` , so neither step touches the other’s output. If one step ever consumes the other’s output, make it depend on that step directly.


```text
mise   tasks            # lists install, build:content, build
mise   run   build        # npm ci + Python step, then vite build
```


The[running tasks guide](https://mise.jdx.dev/tasks/running-tasks.html) sets the default limit at eight parallel jobs.


## Per-Project Env Vars With mise


Values in the` \[env\]` table are plain text in a committed file. mise env is configuration management, not secret management. In the example, the Python script reads` CONTENT_DIR` through` os.environ` , and the frontend reads` import.meta.env.VITE_SITE_NAME` .


The` VITE_` prefix makes the risk of plaintext` \[env\]` values concrete. The[Vite env docs](https://vite.dev/guide/env-and-mode) explain that any variable starting with` VITE_` ends up in the client bundle, with its value written into the code at build time. Any` VITE_` value in` mise.toml` is public once the site ships.


A missing build-time variable does not fail the build. You get a bundle that calls the wrong URL. Session replay can show this from the user’s side: you watch requests go to an` undefined` base URL, then trace the problem back to the environment the build ran in.


## When Is mise Worth It?


If a project only needs Node, nvm and an` .nvmrc` already do the job, and mise is optional. The nvm guides cover that setup well. mise is worth adopting when one repository pins two or more runtimes and CI has to match every laptop. To try it on a repo you already have, add a` mise.toml` with` \[tools\]` pins, run` mise lock` , commit both files, and change your CI build step to` mise run build` .


## FAQs


Where should I keep secrets if mise.toml is committed?


Keep secrets in a gitignored mise.local.toml, or declare them in mise.toml with required = true, which makes mise check that the variable is set without storing a value. Adding redact = true masks values in captured task output, but mise env still prints them in plaintext. For secrets that must be committed, mise can decrypt SOPS files encrypted with age (an experimental feature) for mise exec, tasks and shell activation.


Does mise read asdf .tool-versions files?


Yes. Unlike .nvmrc, mise reads .tool-versions without any extra settings. On Unix it can also run asdf shell plugins, though not every asdf command or plugin is guaranteed to work. If mise.toml and .tool-versions in the same directory declare the same tool, mise.toml wins. The mise docs advise against sharing install directories between asdf and mise, so run mise install after you switch.


Why does my editor or script use a different Node version than my terminal?


Editors, git hooks and schedulers often don't load your interactive rc file, so the mise activation hook never runs. To fix this, add mise activate zsh --shims (or the line for your shell) to a login profile your editor reads, such as ~/.zprofile, and keep plain mise activate in ~/.zshrc. For scripts, use mise exec -- command or mise run instead. Shim mode skips some activation features, such as most hooks.
